Through a review of legal disputes, existing cost allocation practices, and regional case studies, we identify cost allocation trends and potential strategies to minimize cost allocation disputes for future projects. Transmission projects advance most effectively when regions use flexible, easy-to- apply methods, evaluate benefits relative to costs across portfolios, and actively engage stakeholders to ensure broadly distributed benefits and support. The six regional project case studies revealed common trends and lessons learned for transmission cost allocation. These include lessons on the planning approach used to identify and evaluate projects and the actual cost allocation method design. Lessons learned for transmission cost allocation Regional transmission planners use discretion granted through federal regulations to develop a range of cost allocation methods. Regional transmission planners have used the discretion granted through Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 1000 to adopt diverse approaches to allocate costs for transmission projects, reflecting regional preferences and system conditions. To allow comparisons across regions, we develop a cost allocation taxonomy whereby we group transmission projects and cost allocation methods into six project types and five cost allocation approaches. Figure ES-2 compares the cost allocation approaches used by each region. CAISO = California Independent System Operator; ERCOT = Electric Reliability Council of Texas; ISO-NE = ISO New England; MISO = Midcontinent Independent System Operator; NYISO = New York Independent System Operator; PJM = PJM Interconnection; SPP = Southwest Power Pool Successful cost allocation methods strike a balance between precision and practicality. The review of legal disputes over transmission cost allocation and project case studies reveals successful cost allocation methods are both detailed enough to ensure costs are allocated to project beneficiaries and feasible to implement in a real system. This tension appears primarily in relation to (1) identifying project beneficiaries and (2) quantifying project costs and benefits. Current regulations allow discretion in implementing cost allocation methods, provided these decisions are evidence based, cost and benefits are relatively balanced, costs are assigned to project beneficiaries, and the analytic cost allocation methods roughly identify project beneficiaries given future uncertainties and imperfect analytical tools. The most successful application of benefit evaluation in our case studies was for the purposes of project selection and communication with stakeholders, not cost allocation.
